title: The sanctuary (Gaudium et Spes 16)
hookLine: conscience is the most secret core and sanctuary of a person
tomorrow: who shows you what a human being is meant to be?

cards: Something broke, and it's your call whether to say so. The group chat has an opinion. A search bar has an opinion.
Somebody's video, with good lighting, has an opinion. Then it's late, the phone is face down on the nightstand, and there's one voice left, the one nobody else can hear.
The same council document gives the place that voice speaks a church name. It calls it a sanctuary.

teach.b: Paragraph sixteen starts deep inside a person. There, it says, each of us finds a law we didn't write for ourselves, and still have to obey.
Its voice keeps calling us to love what is good and avoid what is evil, and when it matters it speaks plainly: do this, shun that.
The council says this law is written by God in the human heart, an echo of Paul's letter to the Romans, and that obeying it is the very dignity of a person. Then the image.

Conscience, it says, is the most secret core and sanctuary of a person, where they are alone with God, whose voice echoes in their depths. In a church, the sanctuary is the holy space around the altar.
The council puts one inside every human being. So conscience isn't the same as a mood, or whatever feels least stressful at midnight.

teach.h: NOT A MOOD: A VOICE HEARD HONESTLY.
teach.b: It's a law you didn't invent, heard honestly. And the council is careful. Conscience can get things wrong.
When it errs out of an ignorance a person couldn't overcome, it keeps its dignity. It's different when someone stops caring what is true and good, or when a habit of sin slowly dims it.
So the paragraph asks two things at once: listen to that voice, and keep it clear.
It adds that being faithful to conscience joins Christians with everyone else searching for what is true.

how: Catholics are taught to form their conscience and follow it, and many examine their conscience in quiet before confession or at the end of the day.

o: a safe shelter offered to someone in danger
conscience: the inner place where you're alone with God
the area around an altar where only clergy may stand

p: not written by us, still obeyed
where a person is alone with God

s: conscience is just the guilty feeling after you do something wrong
the council calls it a law we didn't write, calling us to good before we act.
Gaudium et Spes says conscience can err and still keep its dignity
when it errs from an ignorance a person couldn't overcome.
following conscience sets Christians apart from everyone else
fidelity to conscience joins Christians with others in the search for truth.

games.q: at your part-time job, the manager says to mark yesterday's pastries as fresh. everyone else does it. by Gaudium et Spes 16, where does the decision get made?
o: in the sanctuary: alone with God, asking what is good.
with the coworkers: if everyone does it, it's fine.
with the manager: an order takes away your part in it.
games.why: the council puts the decision in conscience, the sanctuary where a person is alone with God and hears a law they didn't write: do good, avoid evil.

practice: Close your eyes and bring one choice in front of you to mind, even a small one. Let the other voices go quiet, one at a time, and ask only: what is the good thing here? Then wait, and listen.

wordCard.voice: The sanctuary. Gaudium et Spes's name for conscience: the inmost place where a person is alone with God.

orig.note: Latin for conscience, the word the council's Latin text uses.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: alone with God, where a law you didn't write still speaks plainly. Rest well.
